doc.title: Language Features
doc.paragraph: In this section, you will be guided through the features of Adaptive Script and how they compare and contrast to other languages, such as ECMAScript.

Variables in Adaptive Script are used to identify a memory location, and are declared using the let or const keywords. Unlike ECMAScript, Adaptive Script does not support the var keyword, which has semantics surrounding its scope that are not compatible with how Adaptive Script processes variables.

Adaptive Script does not have support for classes. This means that the ECMAScript classes such as Array, Object, Integer, String, Boolean, Symbol, Map, Error, Exception, etc. cannot be used in Adaptive Script.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support importing code from other locations. The only way to share code between scripts is to store them in qualified variables that would be accessible to scripts.

Adaptive Script can annotate values with Adaptive data types (integer, string, arrays, object shapes, unions, and more). Annotations are always accepted; optional type checking (off by default) can catch mismatches at compile time and/or runtime. See the language reference for syntax and flags.
Adaptive Script does not have support for prototypal inheritance.

ECMAScript has a feature called closure, which allows a function to access variables that are defined outside of its scope, and retain the values that were bound to those variables at the time of its scope creation.
At this time, Adaptive Script does not provide closure features.

There are two import differences between Adaptive Script and ECMAScript as it relates to statements. In ECMAScript, semicolons are optionally used to separate statements. In Adaptive Script, they are required.
Furthermore, in ECMAScript, any expression can be used as statements and in Adaptive Script, this is not allowed.
Adaptive Script provides try/throw/catch/finally exception handling, but the syntax and the objects are different than those in ECMAScript.
In Adaptive Script, throw is a statement that requires a string (the error message) and an optional data to allow users to pass along contextual data to the exception handler.

In ECMAScript, the catch statement accepts any value that was thrown, including an Error object, but in Adaptive Script, a single object is always caught, which contains the message and data that was thrown. The catch binding may be a simple name or a list/object Pattern (same destructuring as let / const), for example catch ({ message, data }).

Function and lambda parameters may be a simple name or the same list/object Pattern used in let / const (holes, defaults, rest, rename, nesting, string keys, and computed keys). Parameter defaults may be any Expression. At a call site, f(...array) expands an array into separate arguments (in addition to definition-side ...rest formals). See the Language Reference Function statement for examples.

Object and array behavior is provided by Adaptive functions in the environment, not by methods on shared type objects. Optional method-style calls such as obj->keys() or arr->push(1) are available when a function is a data-type method (the receiver is the first parameter).

Helpers include property listing (keys, values, entries), indexing (at), stack and queue mutators (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice), immutability (freeze), and quantifiers (every / some, same family as all_of / any_of). See the Language Reference section Objects and Arrays and the Function Reference categories object, array, and higher_order_array.

Object property names in an object value may be an identifier, a string literal, or an expression in square brackets. Bracket expressions are evaluated when the object value is evaluated; the result is used as the property name (a string). This is the same idea as obj[expression] for get and assignment. Variable and parameter names remain lexical identifiers.
Adaptive Script does not support the new and delete keywords.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support generators or user-defined iterators. Arrays can be iterated with for-of. Objects are iterated by walking keys, values, or entries (for example for (let pair of entries(o))).
At this time, Adaptive Script does not support asynchronous operations.
The this keyword in ECMAScript has no meaning in Adaptive Script.
The eval function in ECMAScript allows a programmer to execute a string as if it were code. In Adaptive Script, this is accomplished using the evaluate function, which has some differences.
In Adaptive Script, any code inside an evaluate call may not access or change any variables outside of its scope.
Adaptive Script does not support the for .. in and all of its semantics.
Adaptive Script supports the ECMAScript switch statement and even has some additional features, such as the ability to use functions to compare values matching a case.
Several Adaptive functions turn values into strings for different purposes. They are easy to confuse.

list.item: stringify produces pure JSON text from an evaluated value. Adaptive data types use their JSON primitive (for example, base64Binary and date become JSON strings). An optional second parameter is a replacer function or an array of property names; an optional third parameter controls whitespace. Use this when you need portable JSON (for example, to store a sealed crypto object).

decompile produces Adaptive text that represents the value as the compiler sees it (calls, blocks, and some #… forms). It is not a pretty-print of the original source, and it is not JSON. Prefer decompile when you need that Adaptive form (including for recompile of many constructs).

A compiler listing is produced when you pass a listing or whitespace argument to compile (for example compile<script>(source, 2)), including from Fiddle. The listing interleaves source with a value tree and includes symbol tables. It is for human understanding of what was compiled, not for recompile or for JSON.

For binary data, decode_to_string interprets octets as UTF-8 text (and fails if the octets are not valid UTF-8). The string conversion of binary is a printable base64 or hex form of the octets, not the UTF-8 of those bytes.

doc.paragraph: Function signatures and full parameter descriptions appear under the Function Reference (categories such as compiler and polymorphic methods on binary types).
You may write #compile in a script to change type-checking options for that script. See Types for the options and examples. For everyday use, prefer the environment flags described there.

You may also see other names that begin with # in the output of decompile when a compiled construct has no ordinary Adaptive Script surface form. Examples include #block, #assignment_target, #list_expression, #script_function, #template_definition, #switch_default, and #statements. They are mentioned here only so that output is recognizable; you write normal Adaptive Script and do not code these forms yourself.

A few names may appear for display only and cannot be recompiled from decompile text (for example #closure_binding and #function_thunk). Compiler listings may also show related structure for humans; again, that is not source you write.
